parents.criterion: Count of enumerated evaluation settings and resource markers
parents.instruction: Score 0-10 by counting or estimating how many distinct evaluation settings and resource markers the abstract enumerates. Count mentions of: named or counted datasets or benchmarks; tasks; languages; domains; model architectures or model families; model sizes or parameter counts; transfer, zero-shot, or cross-lingual settings; numbers of baselines compared; and explicit scale statements such as compute used, number of runs, or number of human raters. 0 = the abstract names no evaluation setting at all. 2 = one setting is named. 5 = roughly three or four distinct settings or counts are named. 8 = five to eight are named, or explicit large counts appear. 10 = the abstract enumerates many settings, or states large counts across several of these categories. This is explicitly NOT a quality judgement. Do not decide whether the coverage is adequate, necessary, convincing, or excessive; do not consider whether anything informative was learned in those settings; do not consider whether the comparisons were controlled. Score only how much enumeration is present in the text.

parents.criterion: Extent of formal notation and mathematical vocabulary
parents.instruction: Score 0-10 the raw extent of mathematically formal vocabulary and notation in the abstract text. Count or estimate the presence of: words such as theorem, lemma, proposition, corollary, proof, bound, convergence, rate, assumption, regularity, convexity, optimality, complexity, and similar formal-mathematical vocabulary; and any inline mathematical notation such as Greek letters, single-letter variable names, subscripts or superscripts, norms, expectations, probability symbols, big-O expressions, inequalities, or displayed formulas. 0 = the abstract contains none of these markers at all. 3 = one or two isolated markers. 7 = markers recur in several sentences. 10 = the abstract is dense with such vocabulary and notation from start to finish. This is explicitly NOT a quality judgement. Do not consider whether the formalism is correct, rigorous, necessary, well used, or informative; do not consider whether the paper actually proves anything; do not consider whether the notation is defined. Score only how much of this vocabulary and notation is present on the page.
